options: It uses a Box observation space instead of Discrete
Its dynamics or reward function change over time for reasons independent of the agent's own actions, such as other agents simultaneously learning
It has more than one possible starting state
It uses reward shaping
questions.explain: Non-stationarity means the environment's dynamics or rewards drift for reasons outside the agent's control, violating the fixed-MDP assumption behind standard RL algorithms.

questions.q: What is partial observability (a POMDP), and what is the typical symptom?
options: The action space is continuous instead of discrete; symptom is slow training
The current observation doesn't contain everything needed to act optimally, often requiring memory of past steps; symptom is a policy that plateaus well below the task's apparent difficulty
The reward is sparse; symptom is zero learning signal early on
The environment has no render mode; symptom is an inability to debug visually
questions.explain: A POMDP's current observation alone is insufficient to act optimally — for example, a single frame can't reveal velocity. A plateauing policy despite more training is a classic symptom, since more training can't substitute for missing information.

questions.q: Why is the fix for partial observability architectural (e.g. stacking frames, adding recurrence) rather than more training or reward tuning?
options: Because reward tuning always makes partial observability worse
Because no amount of training can let a policy infer information that was never present in its observation at all
Because partial observability only occurs in vectorized environments
Because recurrence is required by the Gymnasium API for all environments
questions.explain: If the needed information isn't in the observation, training longer against the same insufficient input can't recover it — the architecture itself needs to incorporate history (e.g., frame stacking or recurrent state).

questions.q: According to the pre-training checklist in this lesson, what should you try to do regarding reward-hacking surface before training?
options: Disable all logging to save compute
Try to find a reward-hacking exploit yourself before training finds it for you
Always use a non-stationary reward
Skip the environment checker to save time
questions.explain: Proactively searching for a sequence of actions that scores high without accomplishing the real task is cheaper than discovering a reward-hacking exploit after a long training run.

questions.q: Why is sparse reward listed as a 'pitfall' rather than just an inherent property of some tasks?
options: Because sparse reward is always a bug in the Gymnasium library
Because reward density is often a design choice, and defaulting to reward-only-at-the-end without considering alternatives has a large, avoidable cost in training compute
Because sparse reward cannot be addressed by reward shaping
Because sparse reward only matters in vectorized environments
questions.explain: Every environment designer makes a choice about how much signal to expose. Treating sparse-reward-at-the-end as the unavoidable default, without asking whether safer partial credit is possible, is the pitfall.
